How Tidal Power Plants Store Energy

By Mara Lindqvist

Share on Twitter Share on Facebook

Tidal lagoons hold water behind a wall at high tide, then release it through turbines once the sea has dropped, which lets operators time their output to demand rather than to the moon.

Unlike a run-of-river dam, a lagoon can pump extra water in at high tide using surplus grid power, and recover it later with interest, because the head it falls through is larger on the way out.

Advertisement

Two-way turbines

Bulb turbines in modern barrages generate on both the flood and the ebb tide. Reversing the blade pitch, rather than the water, keeps the mechanical design simple and the efficiency above eighty percent in both directions.

  • Ebb generation produces about two thirds of annual output.
  • Flood generation fills the remaining third.

The tide is the most predictable renewable resource we have.
